article.title: A New International Order? Xi, Trump & Putin Hold Historic Trilateral Summit in China
article.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. NERMEEN SHAIKH : We begin today’s show looking at today’s historic trilateral summit in China between Chinese President Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The three leaders met for about 90 minutes. After the meeting, Chinese state media issued what it described as a, quote, “peace declaration” by the Chinese, Russian and U.S. leaders. The four-point declaration called for reforms at the United Nations and said the three leaders, quote, “concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.” The three countries are not signatories to the ICC . The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes committed in Ukraine. The declaration also states, quote, “The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.” In addition, the declaration states, quote, “The three countries will engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation.” AMY GOODMAN : Prior to the closed-door meeting, the three leaders shared brief remarks. This is Chinese President Xi Jinping. PRESIDENT XI JINPING : [translated] This is the first time the leaders of our three countries have come together. It is a historic meeting. We will discuss how to safeguard world peace and promote strategic stability and relations among major powers. … The world is undergoing rapid changes unseen in a century. The world is not peaceful, and challenges reveal true leadership. As major world powers and permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, our three nations should lead by example, collaborate to address global challenges, jointly safeguard world peace and stability, and make more significant contributions to the progress of humanity. AMY GOODMAN : Russian President Vladimir Putin also spoke before the trilateral meeting in China. PRESIDENT VLADIMIR PUTIN : [translated] For my part, I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, and our respective peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening global security and stability, provided they engage in constructive, partnership-based cooperation rooted in mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests. NERMEEN SHAIKH : And this is President Trump speaking in China before the trilateral meeting. PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : As presidents of three of the world’s largest countries, we have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet. Too often past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And we feel the opposite, and we think that we are sure about that. No problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them, so no peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech. AMY GOODMAN : Well, we’re joined right now by Scott Lucas. He’s a professor of international politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute. Professor Lucas, thanks so much for being with us. First, if you can just talk about the significance of this moment, of these three world leaders coming together for the first time ever in China, President Trump, the Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as the Chinese President Xi Jinping? SCOTT LUCAS : Well, Amy, I think it’s a significant post-1945 moment, which was, you know, the last time that we had great summits, including discussing the future of China, in part because you’re looking at a changed international order. You’re looking at a United States which is no longer the leader of that post-1945 system. You’re looking at a Russia having succeeded the Soviet Union, which is very much tied down by this struggling invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, isolated, in some part, economically and politically because of that invasion, struggling to escape that isolation. And you’re looking at, I think, what is the most important takeaway, both symbolically and in real terms, from the summit, which is an ascendant China. It was China that really set the terms of what was said throughout this, beyond Ukraine, talking more about the global situation in a couple of ways. They did that symbolically by putting Xi right at the center, as you saw at that table, between Putin and Trump. China now is a great power. But they also did it with the specific terms that they put forward: strategic stability, unity, technology and innovation, and perhaps most striking, free trade — given that, of course, the United States had premised its post-1945 position on precisely that, but you have a Trump administration doing something much differently. There’s a lot of specific takeaways, especially because Donald — because Putin’s priority was Ukraine, but this was a summit where you had Trump coming there for ego and the photo opportunity, Putin because of the problems with his invasion and trying to get an alliance with Trump to force Ukraine’s surrender, and China there for strategy, a political, economic and military free hand in pursuing its alternative system. NERMEEN SHAIKH : Well, Professor Lucas, could you comment specifically on some of the remarks that were made by these leaders, what we mentioned in our introduction on the International Criminal Court, as well as — you know, we’re speaking to you — we’re here at COP31 at the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey — this pledge that they would all increase petroleum production? SCOTT LUCAS : So, one of the features where we are now, with the post-1945 system breaking, perhaps broken, is the dismissal of international law. And that is what you saw, on camera, before that closed-door meeting. Vladimir Putin is wanted on war crimes charges, specifically the deportation of Ukrainian children, by the International Criminal Court. He does not want to face those charges. Donald Trump, who wants a friendship with Vladimir Putin, who will be shown in that vivid embrace of Putin — “He is my friend” — was there to carry out Putin’s wishes by saying the International Criminal Court should have no credibility — not even that its decisions can be questioned, it has no credibility. So, that is where we are, between two of the three leading powers, that there is no regard for the International Criminal Court. And the Chinese, of course, have sort of a different approach, because they’re looking for a different type of international system. I think whether you’re at COP31 dealing with specific questions of climate change, or you’re dealing with specific questions of war crimes or broader questions of justice, this is a crisis moment for international law and for the ICC . NERMEEN SHAIKH : And could you comment also on the fact that this meeting comes so soon after Jensen Huang, the chief of Nvidia, was forced to step down after reports of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, in addition to two others in his company? Do you think that’s significant at all? And would it have come up? SCOTT LUCAS : I don’t think it would have come up directly, but I think it’s part of the important backdrop at work here, which is, on the one hand, China is working from a position of leverage — of course, we’ve known this for quite some time — with its possession of rare earth minerals, with its dominance in terms of magnets. But, of course, it needs chips. On the other side, you have a Trump administration which is almost in chaos right now for two very important reasons. First of all, American companies, in this case Nvidia, allegedly, was taking 20% of its revenue from China, despite saying that none of it came from there. Now, that’s a specific gap regarding where you are in terms of AI and technology in the U.S.-versus-China relationship. And that is magnified by the revelation that the Commerce Department did not enforce more than 100 recommended export controls on China-linked firms. So, on the one hand, you have China, which has a very clear policy where it wants to go with tech and AI and with innovation and with control of resources, and you have a Trump administration that’s scrambling and divided over where exactly its position is right now in terms of the relationship with China. Open supply of chips? Export controls? Something in between? Where does it go next? AMY GOODMAN : I also wanted to ask you — at the same time that they’re meeting in Shenzhen in China, Putin and Xi and Trump, you have Jared Kushner and Witkoff meeting with President Zelensky, with other European representatives. The significance of this and what this means? SCOTT LUCAS : There are two different agendas right now in terms of where we go next regarding that invasion of Ukraine. The Russian agenda is to push Ukraine to the side — don’t discuss a ceasefire, don’t discuss security guarantees for Kyiv, don’t discuss freezing the frontlines; instead, call for a Europe-wide security architecture, by which the Russians mean security guarantees for us, and NATO withdrawing to its 1997 position, which not only means, of course, that Ukraine is exposed. It means that there’s no NATO , effectively, in the Baltic states or in Poland. On the other hand, you have Ukraine and Europe that are saying, “No. Before you discuss a European-wide security arrangement, you need to have a specific commitment to a ceasefire on the current frontlines. You need to have an agreement that Russia will not get more territory. And you need to have security guarantees for Kyiv, so we don’t have a repeat of this aggression.” The problem that we have right now is, is that the Russians are trying to impose their agenda by putting Donald Trump in their pocket. How are they doing that? You saw part of it today from Putin’s rhetoric, and from Trump supporting that rhetoric. But perhaps more seriously, you have it through the Russians putting tens of billions of dollars of proposed economic deals on the table, including some deals that would benefit friends and family of Donald Trump and his envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and saying, “You can get all these deals, provided this invasion is halted on our terms.” AMY GOODMAN : Let me ask you something, and this last question: On the one hand, you have President Trump announcing there shouldn’t be regulation of SI, what he calls superintelligence, but also, will this set a new template for the international order, major powers meeting amongst themselves, ignoring the U.N. Security Council and other forums? We just have a minute, Professor Lucas. SCOTT LUCAS : First of all, Trump’s statement, supported by some of the people in the technological industry, is: “Look, don’t restrict us. Don’t do anything to restrict what we’re doing with AI.” More broadly, what you’re seeing here is this isn’t a question of international order. International order has broken down because certain countries and certain leaders don’t believe in international order. I think that’s true of Vladimir Putin. And with regret, I think that’s also true of Donald Trump and his inner circle. But I think the country that benefits from that lack of respect for international order, and we saw it today, is China. AMY GOODMAN : Professor Scott Lucas teaches international politics at the Clinton Institute, University College Dublin. Coming up, we’re going to go here to Turkey to summarize what’s happening at the U.N. climate summit, in the plenaries, but also outside, where all sorts of groups are protesting all the issues that are being discussed here. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “The Fire of Antalya,” performed at the COP31 opening ceremony. Page 2 This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh. We’re broadcasting from Antalya, Turkey, at the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31. NERMEEN SHAIKH : As we reach the final hours of climate negotiations at this global conference, negotiators have released a second draft text for the final outcome of this year’s COP . Global civil society activists have already criticized the text for stripping out hard-won language on accountability from Global North countries and legal anchors to protect the countries and communities most vulnerable to climate change. AMY GOODMAN : Earlier today, Teresa Anderson, the global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International, said climate negotiations are, quote, “looking bleak.” She criticized the European Union’s climate chief Wopke Hoekstra. TERESA ANDERSON : Before coming to COP , actually, the EU’s climate chief, Hoekstra, said any chance of a deal on new climate finance is “dead in the water.” “Dead in the water.” The more I think about it, the more shocked I am that he used that term, in the aftermath of Nepal, as El Niño floods are happening. I’m shocked that he chose that metaphor. When the next catastrophic flood happens, those words will haunt him. NERMEEN SHAIKH : Democracy Now! also caught up with campaigners who’ve been closely following the negotiations here at COP31. This is Kirtana Chandrasekaran from Friends of the Earth International speaking alongside a protest for just solutions from wealthy countries in the Global North. PROTESTERS : No false solutions! Real solutions now! Real solutions now! No false solutions! No false solutions! KIRTANA CHANDRASEKARAN : I’m Kirtana Chandrasekaran with Friends of the Earth International. I was at the “divan” meeting last night, and the divan is supposed to be a roundtable for leaders, but there was no leadership in the room. And all we saw is the Global North countries abandoning their moral and legal commitments, country after country saying that “we are worried about breaching 1.5,” with no irony about how we’ve got here, which is 30 years of inaction on their part, and the solution for that being so-called clean electrification. And what we can see happening now, under the guise of clean electrification, we are seeing many, many new gas plants to electrify data centers. We are seeing many, many new coal plants in the Global South, a massive push, and nuclear, as well. So, they say the words, but they’re not doing any of it. And so they talk about roadmaps, but what is in the roadmap? You know, they were supposed to mobilize $100 million. If you talk about clean electrification, it requires over $2 trillion of investment just for grids and electricity. AMY GOODMAN : At another protest just this morning, a young activist from Nepal urged people to visit her country to experience what it’s like to live on the frontlines of a climate change-fueled catastrophe. SNEHA RAI : I think everybody here knows about the 26th August, 2026, flood. … This is not a single disaster. I think this is the one disaster that you have reached to you on the further side of the world. But we have been facing this on yearly. Yearly, every year, we have been facing this. We don’t need hope anymore. We don’t need words anymore. We need actions right now. And Nepal is a mountainous country, you know, and we have been saying that we are resilient people. We are resilient, but there is a limit to resilient. AMY GOODMAN : Just some of the voices here at the U.N. climate summit. For more, we’re joined by Luisa Neubauer. She is a climate justice activist, lead organizer of Germany’s Fridays for Future movement. In 2021, she was the lead plaintiff in the landmark Neubauer v. Germany case, which forced the German government to strengthen its national climate protection laws. We welcome you to Democracy Now! here at the U.N. climate summit. Right now as we’re sitting here, the second draft of the — for the final report here has just come out. And I’m wondering if you can talk about the progress that has been made, and not made, what you’re most concerned about, Luisa. LUISA NEUBAUER : Yes, of course. So, this is a conference where we try to solve our existential climate problems. And we do know, we are all aware, that the root cause of that very problem is oil, coal and gas. That’s the fossil fuels. So, now we are faced with a new draft negotiation text where the mention of having to get away from the use and exploitation of oil, coal and gas is being stripped out. So, what are we talking about then? And then, what we do see in the text, which is included, is that Saudi Arabia and some petroleum states have really won big time here, because suddenly there’s inclusion of, I would say, magic technologies sucking CO2 out of the atmosphere, which is mentioned big times. We do know those technologies won’t deliver in scale. We have much better solutions at hand, like renewables. So, we see, really, this is not going well. We are not doing fine. And if anything, after this conference ends, we need people to take the streets and fight for more justice out there. NERMEEN SHAIKH : And also, I mean, you mentioned Saudi Arabia and all these petroleum-producing states. Talk about the IPCC report — LUISA NEUBAUER : Yes. NERMEEN SHAIKH : — which has now been delayed. And what justification was given for its delay? LUISA NEUBAUER : It is a real achievement that everything that is being discussed here in these halls is based on the best available science. That is something people have fought for. It’s a real achievement. And now we’ve seen in recent months that some of the most powerful countries, including the U.S., have been very vocal about kind of boycotting the involvement in the climate science here in these halls. But that means the doors are wide open for all kinds of denial and relativation of what we are seeing here. So, now in the new negotiation text, there is a better, I would say, agreement that we have to have the science in the room, which you can call a achievement. But for me, honestly, that’s a bare minimum. I mean, what are we talking about? If this is about discussing should we have climate science in the room or not, what are we even aiming at? NERMEEN SHAIKH : And, you know, you are from Germany and were one of the lead organizers of the Fridays for Future in Germany. Could you tell us why Germany has changed? It was, as you’ve pointed out, also a climate pioneer. LUISA NEUBAUER : Yeah. NERMEEN SHAIKH : And now it seems to have altered its position, and also, in fact, the entire EU no longer stands where it once did. LUISA NEUBAUER : Yeah. Many of us activists here from, say, EU countries, we are here to really put pressure on our own governments, which are some of the richest countries in the world, who’ve accumulated that very wealth to the cost of others around the globe. That is what we’re seeing, right? They are paying the costs. It is emissions coming from countries like Germany who cause, you know, partly, floods in Nepal. That’s a climate change physics here. So we need these countries to step up. And for a long time, Germany, you know, we have a very vocal climate movement. We have a lot of civil society really taking the streets. So, for a long time, Germany was really moving ahead. Yet, in recent years, we’ve seen a backlash in Germany and other countries. And that is a problem, because we need countries to step up so others can follow. And if even those countries who have the chance to do so, who have technologies at hand, who have enough money to fund, you know, renewables, if they don’t take that lead, who are we expecting to do that? So, that’s why — AMY GOODMAN : And who is most affected by that? LUISA NEUBAUER : Sorry? AMY GOODMAN : When they don’t take the lead. LUISA NEUBAUER : Yes, that’s — who is going to fill that void? And right now we’re seeing that, you know, other countries are taking advantage of that. So, suddenly we see fossil fuel lobbyists having a great time. AMY GOODMAN : Let me ask you about this latest news. EU countries, the European Parliament have agreed to delay by two years rules requiring oil, gas and coal importers to report methane emissions due to energy market disruption linked to the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran. So, they’re using — LUISA NEUBAUER : Yeah. AMY GOODMAN : — the war in Iran as an excuse to say they won’t be reporting their methane emissions. What’s the significance of this? LUISA NEUBAUER : Yeah. So, it sounds very technical, but what we’re seeing, when we tackle the climate crisis, we have a transparency issue. So, everyone is making up their own rules. Everyone is reporting different numbers. And by the end of the day, you don’t know who is responsible for emissions, what do we need to tackle, where are emissions even coming from, and how do we get out of this climate crisis mechanism. So we need real reporting. Yet we find that countries, but also industries, are very good and basically ducking away from that responsibility. And that makes us, you know, blind, in a way, from our own problems. We could be, you know, clear-eyed, steering towards a future that is powered by renewable, that is, you know, producing more justice and a real future, especially for young generation. And instead, we once again see that fossil fuel industries and fossil fuel nations are making the rules, and we all will pay the cost. NERMEEN SHAIKH : Well, one of the words that has been repeated very often here is “electrification,” AI and data centers, of course, but also the transportation sector. And apparently, the very largest, by volume, sources that require electricity is air conditioning. So, if you could talk about the significance? What does it mean to electrify — LUISA NEUBAUER : Yeah. NERMEEN SHAIKH : — places? Where does the energy for that come from? And also the fact — I mean, it is extraordinary. I read these figures that in the U.S. about 90% of households have access to air conditioning. In India, it’s less than 20%, and in Nigeria, it’s about 5%. LUISA NEUBAUER : Yeah. NERMEEN SHAIKH : So, if you could just, I mean, talk about that, air conditioning? Of course, places are getting hotter, including Europe. AMY GOODMAN : And at the same time, you have 50,000 people dying this year of the heat. NERMEEN SHAIKH : Exactly. LUISA NEUBAUER : That is a — that is a real worry. Just a state, you know, what we negotiate here, what we see people talking about, it feels like they’re living on a different planet. This is a planet they negotiate with that waits for us, until we have, you know, agreed on a nitty-gritty paragraph that nobody even understands. Yet the world out there, the world we live on, is a world where we still miss thousands of people from the latest flood in Nepal, and that’s just the latest flood; where thousands, tens of thousands of people died on a privileged continent like Europe because of the heat, and they weren’t protected; where right now our colleagues in Honduras are faced with the consequences of the El Niño phenomenon. That is the real world out there, and for that world, we need to provide solutions. And number one, of course, we need to be fast with whatever we do, because right now we see that the solutions we try to put on the problems are eaten up by the problem. And aircon is a perfect example. It’s getting hotter, so people need more air conditioning. And at the same time, that air conditioning is causing the problem that we’re trying to tackle. We’re not going to get out of this devil’s wheel if we’re not getting faster and better in applying these solutions. And this is why this conference is talking about, rightfully so, to electrify, so to make sure we get away from fossil fuels, from coal, oil and gas, and into electricity powered by renewables, by the sun and by the wind. That is really important. Yet now we see, once again, at this conference that those who are taking the lead in the negotiations, seemingly so, say, “Well, what about we electrify, so we, you know, provide electricity, but, you know, maybe it comes through some fossil fuel gas or from nuclear?” That means we are doing some nice modernization projects, but for that, we don’t need a climate conference, that you can solve an industrial project anywhere. AMY GOODMAN : And let me say that 50,000 number that I said people have died of heat was on Europe alone, and people are saying it’s millions who die of heat-related diseases. But I wanted to end in the last minute by asking you about your landmark Neubauer v. Germany case, which forced the German government to strengthen its national climate protection laws. How old were you when you brought this? LUISA NEUBAUER : I was in my mid-twenties. And this was an amazing, an amazing case for us. We’ve been organizing hundreds of thousands of people to take the streets in Germany alone, but, I mean, we were all over the world. And it really proved people power works and activism works. And I find we forget that these days, that it matters where we show up, how we show up, how often we show up, that it matters most that we show up in dark times, but it’s not all easy, easy-peasy, and it’s not all flowing. And what we did, once we took the streets with so many people, and we still saw the German government not acting in time, we took the courts. The courts alone won’t solve the crisis we’re in, but they are crucial mechanisms, and we must make use of that. And then we go back to the streets, and we make sure we are everywhere. We’re showing up again and again and again. And right now we see some of the richest billionaire people on the planet, some of the most powerful countries wanting to put this dystopian future upon us. And I guess it’s a good time to choose our own future and stand up for what we believe in. AMY GOODMAN : Luisa Neubauer, we want to thank you so much for being with us, climate justice activist, lead organizer of Germany’s Fridays for Future movement, in 2021 the lead plaintiff in the landmark Neubauer v. Germany case, which forced the German government to strengthen its national climate protection laws. Coming up, we speak to Indigenous activists, one from Alaska. We’ll talk about the climate crisis and the election of Mary Peltola, who just made history for being the first Alaskan Native elected to the U.S. Senate. And then we’ll turn to Russia, where an Indigenous activist was arrested right after returning from COP30, the U.N. climate summit in Brazil. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “The Fire of Antalya,” performed at the COP31 opening ceremony here in Antalya, Turkey. Page 3 Democrat Mary Peltola was declared the winner this week of Alaska’s closely watched race for U.S. Senate, making her the first Alaska Native lawmaker elected to the upper chamber of Congress. At the COP31 climate conference in Turkey, we speak with Aakaluk Adrienne Blatchford, an Inupiaq and Yup’ik organizer from Unalakleet, Alaska. She says Peltola’s win is a significant milestone for Indigenous peoples in Alaska. “Having somebody represent us in such a large capacity with such a big weight on her shoulders, but still carrying that struggle with her as she continues to advocate for our people and our way of life, is monumental,” says Blatchford.
